data.scope: Paid third-party application families and hardware qualified for Logix or explicitly supported non-Logix configurations. This is not the entire worldwide CP/M catalogue or installed base. Logix/AION products and operating systems are excluded; independent BPI is included once.
counting: CP/M applications includes the TUI-aware subset; never add those columns. AIONix means native ERA editions only; legacy Z80 execution on a coprocessor remains CP/M.

A product family is one title per target, regardless of version, language or disk format. Cross-target families are deduplicated in the unique-family total. BPI modules and suite count as one family/customer licence.
Copies sold are paid end-customer licences in that quarter, including paid OEM licences; free copies, piracy, patches and bundled Logix/AION apps are excluded. Cumulative copies are separate.

Manufacturers and models are available at quarter-end. Sales are units during the quarter. OEM computers are shown separately from accessories; totals combine both disjoint groups. No retirements of titles/models are assumed during this short horizon.

Hardware model IDs represent qualified configurations. Different connectors/CPU cards require separate qualification; a driver-only update is not a new model. Anonymous supplier/title cohorts quantify a market, not invented named contracts.
data.uncertainty: Judgmental scenarios, not confidence intervals. Logix host shipments match sales_forecast.json for every scenario through 1983. From January 1982 the five signed clone cohorts replace North Star/Vector prospects; other OEM prospects remain separate and never become Logix computer receipts.

readiness.assessment: Existing CP/M character/file interfaces offer the fastest route. Launch Simple C and SDK establish a contemporary C subset, shared TUI headers and resource tests. Early compiler/runtime defects and 48/64 KB limits keep third-party TUI uptake gradual.

DRI extensions release May 5; published profiles, reference drivers and clinics widen the addressable market. Tandy Model II support starts October 15. Other OEMs remain prospects. Native Apple II cards provide hardware access, not CP/M execution.

Full dual-target compiler/IDE/framework releases May 19, 1980. Native application supply ramps over several quarters. Portable C/TUI projects can share logic, but need file/memory adapters, 16-to-32-bit width review, rebuild and regression tests. Assembly-heavy products usually retain CP/M compatibility editions first.

Assumed improvements in diagnostics, ABI stability, libraries and conformance raise port completion. AIONix grows from a smaller base. IBM PC/DOS competition and established Abacus/BPI offerings limit rival business applications; conservative adoption models slower recruitment.

Published and forward-compatible architecture; finish connector/power drawings, wire byte order, class profiles and electrical tests before shipment. V1 is point-to-point, quiescent attach; maximum 50 KB/s before overhead. Printers and serial adapters arrive before complex storage and instruments.

Monitor capability negotiation and raster profiles are documented, but voltage/connector/timing and readability need qualification. Monitor I cannot acquire Monitor II resolution by software. Internal cards are platform-specific; Aurelia, Artemis, Apple II and S-100 need distinct electrical/mechanical adapters, ROM/driver ABI and timing tests.

popular_hardware.priority: Highest volume: forms, accounting and correspondence

popular_hardware.likely_products: External floppy units, backup drives and later hard-disk subsystems
popular_hardware.route: FlexiBUS block protocol for modest throughput; native internal controller for faster storage
popular_hardware.priority: High: capacity and backup; boot/media/error semantics remain gates

popular_hardware.route: Separate Aurelia and Artemis board variants; Apple II/S-100 host adapters for external ecosystem access
popular_hardware.priority: High: practical business upgrades; shared protocol does not imply shared card pinout

popular_hardware.route: New serial/modem class, flow control and modem-status driver; higher-level protocol testing

popular_hardware.likely_products: Plotters, digitizers, barcode readers, laboratory I/O and instrument interfaces

historical_sources.title: Dennis Ritchie, The Development of the C Language
historical_sources.use: Primary author account: C portability work and pre-standard language context. Does not establish fictional compiler maturity.

historical_sources.use: Compiler author dates commercial release to August 1979 and describes a pre-standard C subset for CP/M. Its lifetime sales are not used as annual Logix demand.

historical_sources.use: Background for WordStar as an existing CP/M candidate; all Logix qualification dates and forecast ranks are counterfactual.

compatibility_pool.basis: Scenario assumptions for discoverable distinct CP/M application families, not measured historical totals or confirmed Logix qualifications. Historical CP/M software is available beyond explicitly named products.
compatibility_pool.counting: Use max(existing installed-base qualification curve, qualified legacy pool), never add the pools. TUI is a subset; an ERA native port is a separate edition of the same family. Source rights, disk/terminal compatibility, RAM and support are required.
compatibility_pool.sales_treatment: Application availability is not an extra paid licence or hardware sale. Existing purchase budgets and Logix demand factors already recognise compatibility and software benefits; no second blanket sales multiplier.
compatibility_pool.partner_support: Published interfaces, sample drivers, conformance tests, loan hardware, joint demonstrations, Academy training and stable C/TUI APIs support the qualification fraction. Higher fraction represents stronger execution, not signed deals with the illustrative vendors.

historical_sources.claim: CP/M interface and system conventions underpin compatibility assessment, not automatic hardware-independent execution.
BDS C author records a CP/M C compiler from 1979; this supports a contemporary developer base, not measured Logix compiler superiority.
